title: data_table: assorted improvements and fixes
description:
Hello! I've been working on the translation of the data_table cheatsheet, and noticed what seems to be some room for improvements or fixes. Specifically:

1. The homepage link points to an obsolete wiki. Please link to [https://r-datatable.com]().
2. The vignette link points to the functions reference. Perhaps link to the intro vignette?
3. The text boxes with subtitles are set up so that, when you start changing the title (eg for translation) it increases or decreases in size around its center. Ideally it should do so keeping its left margin were it is. In LibreOffice Impress, backtranslating from my native language, this option can be found in menu Format / Text box and shapes / Text attributes... And then, in the Text tab, select the left margin (or perhaps upper left corner) as the text anchor.
4. The text boxes with subtitles should be formatted with text in all upper case, so that you type with title case or sentence case but it is displayed in all upper case. This should improve accessibility (screen readers), spell checking and make it easier for anyone copying-and-pasting said subtitles.
5. The table describing the arguments to melt() has a mismatch between apparent and actual rows. Please make sure each argument/description is in its own row.
6. [edit] Also, there are two data.table cheatsheets ("datatable" and "data_table"), perhaps make sure the new version is the only one.

By the way, data.table 1.16 is due soon

title: All: Inadequate German translation of “Cheat Sheet”
description:
Disclaimer: I am not a linguist.

As a German native speaker, it repeatedly strikes me as very odd when international communities translate the term “cheat sheet” into German “Schummelzettel”. It's a very literal (and thus, not incorrect) translation, but it always feels very much “machine translated”¹ – I never heard anyone saying it. I think I first read the term in tech projects that publish these, whereas at school they were called “Spickzettel”, which is what I would suggest as a proper translation.

The two largest German dictionaries (Duden and Wahrig) both only contain _Spickzettel_, but not _Schummelzettel_. Same for the [historical dictionary by the Brothers Grimm](https://woerterbuchnetz.de/?sigle=DWB&lemid=S34294), and the DWDS contains both but documents a higher word frequency for [Spickzettel](https://www.dwds.de/wb/Spickzettel) than for [Schummelzettel](https://www.dwds.de/wb/Schummelzettel), as does the Corpora Collection Leipzig ([Spickzettel](https://corpora.uni-leipzig.de/de/res?corpusId=deu_newscrawl-public_2018&word=Spickzettel) vs. [Schummelzettel](https://corpora.uni-leipzig.de/de/res?corpusId=deu_newscrawl-public_2018&word=Schummelzettel)).

¹ Though both Google Translate and DeepL translate _cheat sheet_ to _Spickzettel_. [According to Wiktionary](https://de.wiktionary.org/wiki/Schummelzettel), _Schummelzettel_ could be an Austrian term.

title: teachR cheat sheet should use proper Bloom's Taxonomy objectives
description:
I came across the teachR cheat sheet because I wanted to get to the tidyr cheat sheet and I avoided reading the filename. I believe that this cheat sheet needs some attention because many modern courses on R are tailored towards the taxonomy categories "create", "evaluate" and "analyse" rather than the other end. This also goes for the books on r4ds, tidytextmining, and ggplot2. Since this is particularly good practice for novices, the teachR cheat sheet should not propagate otherwise. From this viewpoint the related objective should be rephrased to *"Learners will **integrate** the principles of reactivity while **building** a simple application"*, which translates "integrate" to 4.1/4.2 (Analyse+Differentiating/Organising) and "build" to 6.3 (Create+Produce) within Bloom's Taxonomy. 

The cheat sheet also contains a colourful triangle. It states next to it "Bloom's Taxonomy". I know the triangle is taken from  https://cft.vanderbilt.edu/. Yet, it is strongly discouraged to use the triangle visualisation for the "Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing" (Anderson et al., 2001). In fact, none of the five original books on the Taxonomy contains, mentions or even suggests any triangles. On page 90f of the abridged edition of Anderson et al. (2001) it is made very clear that a unit of learning at any level is *not* constrained to one certain set of categories but can span across the entire board. I assume that the triangle relates to the origins of other "learning triangles" as reported here: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2018.1518638 

If a triangle must be used then it should be upside down because the Taxonomy consistently refers to the "create" category for the *most* complex cognitive processes and *remember* for the *least* cognitively demanding activities. Please note that greater cognitive complexity means more effective learning.

Moreover, the arrows into the graphic are really irritating as they are pointing to "understand" and "apply", while they really should point to "analyse" and "create", as such learning objective is really proven by analysing and creating something. I know that the words used in the objective show up at these levels in the triangle diagram, which leads to another reason why this diagram should not be used: Several of the terms shown in the triangle do not appear in the Taxonomy. Instead variants of *describe* and *demonstrate* appear across all Taxonomy categories (btw. this is also elaborated and visible on the page that has the triangle at the beginning).  Really, the triangle is very much not helpful. 

A proper learning objective for the levels on the  cheat sheet would be "Learners will explain the key principles of reactivity and use the related functions for extending an existing application". **Oof** this does not come easy. Strictly speaking this is already half way in "creating" or "evaluating" in terms of the Taxonomy. description:
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/26348643/r-regex-with-stringi-icu-why-is-a-considered-a-non-punct-character?noredirect=1&lq=1

Some of the characters listed under `[:punct:]` on the sidebar should actually be listed under `[:symbol:]`, a class that isn't mentioned. The characters currently listed work in base-R regex, but not `stringr`.

``` r
stringr::str_extract_all(
  "! # $ % & ' ( ) * + , - . / : ; < = > ? @ [ \ ] ^ _ ` { | } ~", 
  "[[:punct:]]+"
  )
#> [[1]]
#>  [1] "!" "#" "%" "&" "'" "(" ")" "*" "," "-" "." "/" ":" ";" "?" "@" "[" "]" "_"
#> [20] "{" "}"

stringr::str_extract_all(
  "! # $ % & ' ( ) * + , - . / : ; < = > ? @ [ \ ] ^ _ ` { | } ~", 
  "[[:symbol:]]+"
)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "$" "+" "<" "=" ">" "^" "`" "|" "~"
```

named_mean <- function(data, var, name) {

  var <- rlang::enquo(var)
  data %>% 
    summarise(!!name := mean(!!var))
}
